howItWorks.intro: This calculator layers three inputs — current elevation, a chosen emissions scenario, and a target year — onto NOAA's published sea level rise curves, then checks the result against a storm surge allowance to produce a flood margin and a risk label.
rules: Rise is interpolated along NOAA's 2022 scenario curves rather than a straight line from a 2020 baseline to the 2100 endpoint, since ice-sheet contributions accelerate instead of growing at a constant rate
Scenario endpoints by 2100: Low ≈1 ft (0.3 m), Moderate ≈2 ft (0.6 m), High ≈4 ft (1.2 m), Extreme ≈6.5 ft (2.0 m) — spanning the IPCC likely range plus its low-confidence high-end tail

A storm surge allowance (roughly 3–15+ ft depending on storm category and local bathymetry) is added on top of the baseline projection, because the worst coastal flooding happens when a surge rides on an already-elevated sea, not during calm weather
howItWorks.outro: These figures describe open-ocean projections only. Your actual exposure also depends on local subsidence or uplift, levees and seawalls, and the shape of your specific shoreline — none of which a global curve can capture, so treat the output as a starting estimate rather than a substitute for a site-specific flood study.

faq.question: How much is global sea level actually projected to rise by 2100?
faq.answer: IPCC AR6's likely range runs from about 0.28–0.55 m (roughly 1–1.8 ft) under a low-emissions pathway to 0.63–1.01 m (about 2–3.3 ft) under a high-emissions pathway, measured against 1995–2014 levels, with a low-confidence possibility above 1.5 m if West Antarctic ice-sheet collapse accelerates faster than current models capture. The rate is already running near 4 mm/year globally and increasing, and a meaningful amount of this century's rise is already locked in from heat the ocean has absorbed.

faq.question: Why does my local flood risk differ from the global average?
faq.answer: Global figures describe eustatic (ocean-volume) change only. What floods your street is relative sea level — eustatic rise plus local land motion. Coastal Louisiana, parts of Texas, and the Chesapeake subside several millimeters a year from sediment compaction and groundwater withdrawal, roughly doubling or tripling their effective local rise, while parts of coastal Alaska are still rebounding from Ice Age glacial unloading and can see relative sea level hold flat or even fall. That is why FEMA flood maps and nearby tide-gauge records matter more for any one address than a global average ever will.

faq.question: Does this calculator include storm surge?
faq.answer: Yes, as a separate allowance layered on top of the baseline rise projection — surge is a short-lived, event-driven spike, not part of the long-term trend. A Category 3 storm can push surge of roughly 9–12 ft in vulnerable Gulf Coast geography, while a smaller tropical storm might add only 3–5 ft. In the worked example above, a property at 4 ft elevation facing 1.6 ft of projected rise plus a 3.3 ft surge ends up roughly 0.9 ft underwater during that event, even though the long-term rise alone looked manageable.

faq.question: Is this a substitute for a FEMA flood map or elevation certificate?
faq.answer: No. FEMA Flood Insurance Rate Maps and surveyed elevation certificates are the regulatory, legally referenced documents for insurance, permitting, and lending, and they incorporate local topography, levees, and historical flood data at a resolution no global calculator can match. Use this tool to frame a long-range planning question, then confirm anything financially or legally significant against your parcel's actual flood zone designation.

faq.question: How reliable are these numbers?
faq.answer: They're grounded in published NOAA and IPCC scenario curves, but every projection carries real uncertainty — future emissions are a policy choice, not a physical constant, and ice-sheet dynamics in Antarctica remain one of the least-constrained variables in the climate system. Treat the output as a scientifically informed estimate with a wide error range, especially toward the century's end and under the higher-emissions scenarios, not as a prediction of the exact water level at your property in any given year.

howWeCalculate.intro: The math behind this tool has two layers: a long-term trend and a short-term shock. The trend comes from NOAA- and IPCC-derived rise curves for the scenario you pick; the shock is a storm surge allowance layered on top of that new, higher baseline.
steps: Your elevation input is treated as height above the current local mean sea level, the same type of datum NOAA tide gauges and FEMA flood maps reference

The selected scenario's published rise curve is interpolated to your target year — these curves bend upward over time rather than rising at a constant rate, reflecting accelerating ice loss later in the century

The projected rise is subtracted from your elevation to get a baseline margin, then the storm surge allowance is subtracted again to model what a single extreme event could do on top of that already-higher baseline
The remaining margin is translated into a risk label — comfortable freeboard, marginal, or already in deficit — so the figure is easier to act on than a raw number in feet
howWeCalculate.disclaimer: Sea level projections are scientific estimates with real uncertainty ranges, not guarantees — actual outcomes depend on global emissions, ice-sheet behavior current models don't fully resolve, and local land motion this tool doesn't measure. For a property-specific determination, pull your parcel's FEMA Flood Insurance Rate Map zone and, where available, a surveyed elevation certificate; those reflect regulatory flood elevations and local benchmarks, not a global curve.

whenToUse.intro: Reach for this calculator when you want a first-pass read on long-horizon coastal exposure before pulling the heavier data sources that any real transaction or permit will eventually require.
scenarios: Screening a coastal property before a purchase, to see whether its elevation leaves any cushion under a mid-range 2060 or 2100 projection
Comparing how a parcel fares under conservative versus high-emissions scenarios, since insurance and mortgage underwriting increasingly price in the wider range rather than just the median case
Sanity-checking a FEMA flood zone designation or an elevation certificate against a longer planning horizon than the current flood map covers
Explaining why two nearby addresses with similar elevation can face different long-term outlooks once local subsidence or uplift is factored in
Stress-testing a site plan against a storm-surge-on-top-of-rise scenario before finalizing freeboard or first-floor elevation in a coastal building design

sections.title: What "Sea Level Rise" Actually Measures
sections.body: Global mean sea level is the eustatic average height of the ocean surface once tides, waves, and daily weather are averaged out. It rises mainly because warming ocean water expands (thermal expansion) and because ice locked in Greenland, Antarctica, and mountain glaciers melts and drains into the sea. The IPCC's Sixth Assessment Report puts the likely range at roughly 0.28–0.55 m by 2100 under a low-emissions pathway (SSP1-2.6) and 0.63–1.01 m under a high-emissions pathway (SSP5-8.5), measured against a 1995–2014 baseline — with a low-confidence possibility of exceeding 1.5 m if marine ice-cliff instability in West Antarctica unfolds faster than current models assume. NOAA's 2022 Interagency report frames this as five named scenarios — Low, Intermediate-Low, Intermediate, Intermediate-High, and High — which is what this calculator's climate-scenario presets are built from. None of these figures is a forecast; each is a branch of a probability tree, and the branch that plays out depends on how much carbon the world emits between now and the century's end.

sections.title: Global Average vs. the Water at Your Property Line
sections.body: The number that matters for any one parcel is relative sea level, not the global average, and the two can diverge sharply. Relative sea level is global (eustatic) rise plus whatever the land underneath is doing — subsiding, rebounding, or holding steady. Along the Louisiana Gulf Coast, groundwater and oil and gas withdrawal plus natural sediment compaction add roughly 5–10+ mm of subsidence per year on top of global rise, which is a large part of why sections of the Mississippi Delta are drowning two to three times faster than the open ocean is rising. Chesapeake Bay and parts of the mid-Atlantic see comparable compaction-driven subsidence of a few millimeters annually. By contrast, coastal Alaska and the Pacific Northwest are still rebounding from the weight of Ice Age glaciers (glacial isostatic adjustment), and in a few spots the land is rising faster than the ocean, so relative sea level there is effectively falling. A homeowner in Norfolk, Virginia and one in Juneau, Alaska can face opposite long-term trends even when the open-ocean rise they're both exposed to is identical.

sections.title: How Elevation, Projected Rise, and Storm Surge Combine
sections.body: This calculator works from one idea: flood risk is a margin, not a single figure. Take a property's elevation above the current tidal datum, subtract the sea level rise projected for the chosen scenario and year, then subtract an allowance for storm surge, and what remains is freeboard — the vertical buffer between dry land and water. Consider a property sitting at 4 ft (≈1.2 m) above mean sea level. Under NOAA's Moderate scenario, roughly 1.6 ft (≈0.5 m) of rise is projected by 2100. A storm surge of about 3.3 ft (≈1 m) riding on top of that during a single hurricane pushes total water height to roughly 4.9 ft above today's baseline — about 11 inches higher than the property sits now. That's a negative margin: not everyday nuisance flooding, but exactly the combined event that overtops waterfront land that looks fine on a map today. Run the same property through the High or Extreme scenario and the deficit widens further, since the far end of the range is driven by ice-sheet contributions that scale up much faster than the middle of the distribution.

howToSteps.title: Set Your Property's Elevation Above Mean Sea Level
howToSteps.description: Enter height in feet above the local mean sea level datum, ideally pulled from a surveyed elevation certificate or a FEMA flood map panel rather than estimated by eye.

howToSteps.title: Pick an Emissions Scenario
howToSteps.description: Choose Low, Moderate, High, or Extreme to match the NOAA pathway you want to test; running more than one scenario shows how sensitive your margin is to how much the world actually emits.

howToSteps.title: Choose a Planning Horizon
howToSteps.description: Set the target year between 2030 and 2100 — rise curves steepen later in the century, so a 2100 result is not simply double a 2060 one.

howToSteps.title: Run the Calculation
howToSteps.description: Press Calculate to interpolate the chosen rise curve to your target year and layer the storm surge allowance on top of it.

howToSteps.title: Read the Margin, Not Just the Rise Figure
howToSteps.description: The projected rise alone tells you less than the margin — elevation minus rise minus surge — which is what actually determines whether that parcel stays dry during a realistic worst-case event.

tips: Use NAVD88 or your local tidal datum, not an arbitrary ground-level guess — elevation certificates and USGS topographic data report heights against a fixed vertical datum, and mixing datums can throw the margin off by feet rather than inches.

Treat the Low scenario as a floor, not a likely outcome — warming already underway locks in meaningful rise even if emissions stopped today, so planning around the best case alone understates exposure.
Layer in a storm surge figure that matches your coastline's storm history; Gulf and Atlantic hurricane coasts generally need a larger allowance than most Pacific or Great Lakes shorelines.
Re-run the calculator at both 2060 and 2100 for the same scenario — a property with a comfortable margin mid-century can slip into deficit by century's end as the rise curves steepen.

Check whether your area is subsiding or rebounding before trusting the output at face value; a nearby NOAA tide gauge trend can shift relative sea level by several millimeters a year in either direction, which adds up over decades.
